beats.text: In twenty thirteen, archaeologists found a diary in a cave by the Red Sea.
It was written by a man who helped build the Great Pyramid.
For decades, people asked how that was even possible. Some said: aliens.
But the diary is a logbook. Its author, Merer, led about forty boatmen.
So we know what they did: they shipped limestone along the Nile, about two hundred blocks a month.
The stone came from the quarries at Tura, most likely for the pyramid's white outer shell.
It's the oldest inscribed papyrus ever found in Egypt, over four and a half thousand years old.
No aliens. Just a diary, and forty men on a boat.

sources: Diary of Merer (Papyrus Jarf A and B): logbooks of the inspector Merer, found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf on the Red Sea by a French mission under Pierre Tallet; year 27 of Khufu; the team transported white limestone from the Tura quarries to Giza by boat; about 30 blocks of 2–3 t per round trip, about 200 blocks per month, about 40 boatmen; Tallet: most likely for the outer casing of the Great Pyramid. Wikipedia 'Diary of Merer' and references (Tallet 2017, Les papyrus de la Mer Rouge I).
Oldest inscribed papyri found in Egypt, written more than 4,500 years ago: History.com (2016/2025), Tallet & Marouard (2014), Near Eastern Archaeology; National Geographic.
'Some said: aliens' refers to the popular ancient-astronaut claim (e.g. TV series); no evidence supports it.
